title: The third rooms
hookLine: the well-ordered life that can still be a little too careful

cards: Here's a certain kind of person. Up on time. Bills paid.
Goes to Mass, gives to the collection, volunteers twice a year, never raises their voice. A good person, genuinely, with a life organized like a well-kept kitchen drawer.
And yet sometimes, when something is asked that doesn't fit the drawer, a big risk, a messy person, a sudden need, they get very quiet and very reasonable.
Teresa of Ávila built a whole set of rooms in her castle for these good, careful people. She's fond of them. And she's worried about them.

teach.b: First, the praise. The people in the third rooms, Teresa says, have come a long way. They avoid sin, even small ones.
They spend time in prayer. They're kind, they give, they keep their homes and lives in order. She calls this a real blessing, and she means it.

teach.h: THE RICH YOUNG MAN WALKS AWAY.
teach.b: A rich young man comes to Jesus. He's kept every commandment since he was a boy. Jesus invites him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow.
And, in the Douay-Rheims: "when the young man had heard this word, he went away sad: for he had great possessions." Teresa says he stays on her mind the whole time she writes about these rooms.
Good all the way through, and then, at the one moment that asks for everything, a little too careful to let go. Third, the reason.
Their love, she says, isn't yet strong enough to overwhelm their reason. Everything is sensible. Even their penances are as orderly as their lives.
They worry about their health, their reputation, what could go wrong. And when a trial comes, they're surprised and hurt, because they've been so good. Fourth, the way on.
Teresa's advice is humility, and a little daring.
Stop measuring how far you've come. Don't wait until you can see the whole path before taking a step.
Her worry, in a picture: a clean house is a good thing, but love sometimes means opening the door when someone knocks at a bad time. Tidy is good. Tidy is not the same as holy.

how: Catholic retreat leaders often use Teresa's third dwelling places to help faithful, church-going people ask where their good habits have become too cautious, and what generous risk love might ask of them.

games.q: you're the rich young man. you've kept every commandment since you were a boy, and Jesus invites you to sell everything, give to the poor and follow him. what do you do?
o: ask for time to think it over.
games.why: he went away sad, because he had great possessions. Teresa keeps him in mind as she writes about these rooms of good, careful people.

practice: Ask where your life is a little too careful: a gift you keep meaning to give, a person you avoid because they're messy, a yes you keep postponing until things are calmer.
Let one come to mind, and choose one generous thing you could do about it, slightly more than feels sensible. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, just decide.

wordCard.voice: Possessions. What the rich young man couldn't let go of when Jesus asked for everything, and what still holds back careful, orderly lives today. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: young man. Matthew's word for the one who went away sad, the figure Teresa uses for the third rooms.

carryVoice: Your line: tidy isn't holy. A good life is a start, not a stopping place. That's two hundred forty-eight.
